The Weight of Small Things

I keep thinking about the way my grandmother peeled an apple. One continuous spiral, the knife never leaving the fruit, the skin falling in a curl onto the newspaper she'd spread across the kitchen table. She did this every morning for my grandfather, who had diabetes and shouldn't have been eating apples at all, but he loved them, so she peeled them, and he ate them, and she watched him eat them with an expression I couldn't read—was it pride? Resignation? Love?

The kitchen was always cold. Even in August, that house held its breath. The refrigerator hummed a low, constant note that I can still hear when I'm trying to fall asleep, that particular frequency of loneliness.

I was seven when I tried to peel an apple myself. The knife slipped. I cut my thumb, not badly, but enough that my mother had to drive me to the emergency room at St. Mary's, and I remember the fluorescent lights, the smell of antiseptic, the way my mother held my hand in the car and said *don't cry, don't cry, it's just a little cut* as if crying were a choice, as if I could simply decide not to feel the sting.

She never let me try again. I don't know if that was protection or something else. I peeled apples for years after, for myself, for my children, for anyone who asked. I got good at it. The spiral would come off in one piece, thin and translucent, and I'd lay it on the cutting board like a question mark, like a promise.

My daughter hated apples. She would eat the peeling, though, if I saved it for her. She'd take the spiral from my hand and eat it like licorice, her small teeth working at the tough skin, her eyes closed in concentration. I never understood this. I still don't.

---

There's a photograph of me at twelve, standing in front of a waterfall I don't remember visiting. I'm wearing a yellow raincoat that looks too big for me, and I'm smiling in a way that suggests I'm performing happiness for someone. My father took the picture. He took a lot of pictures. He also drank a lot, in the years after, in the years before, I'm not sure which came first. The chicken or the egg. The drinking or the distance.

I found the photograph in a box last spring, the box labeled *MISC* in my mother's handwriting, the letters slanting to the right like they were always in a hurry. I sat on my kitchen floor with the box between my knees and I went through everything. Ticket stubs from movies I don't remember seeing. A recipe for something called *church supper casserole* in my grandmother's looping script. A pressed flower, purple, that crumbled when I touched it. And the photograph, the yellow raincoat, the waterfall, the smile.

I don't know where that girl went. I know she's in here somewhere, in the way I still flinch at sudden noises, in the way I check locks three times, in the way I peel apples in one continuous spiral and lay the skin on the cutting board like a question mark, like a promise.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 3 AM. Every night. A small dog, yappy, insistent, as if the darkness itself were a threat that needed announcing. I used to hate this. I would lie in bed with my pillow over my ears, my heart hammering, waiting for the silence that never came.

Then my neighbor died. Cancer, fast, the kind that doesn't give you time to say goodbye properly. His wife moved to Oregon to be near her sister. The dog went with her. I didn't know they'd taken him. I thought maybe he'd been put down, or run away, or simply stopped barking because there was no one left to hear him.

But last week, a new family moved in. They have a small dog. It barks at 3 AM. I lay in bed and I listened, and I felt something I can only describe as gratitude. The world continues. The dog doesn't know my neighbor is gone. The dog doesn't know anything except that it's dark and it's afraid and it wants someone to come.

I got up and made tea. I sat at my kitchen table and I peeled an apple, slowly, carefully, the way my grandmother did. The spiral came off in one piece. I laid it on the cutting board. I ate the apple in slices, dipped in peanut butter, the way my grandfather used to, though I never saw him do it—my grandmother always brought it to him already prepared, on a plate with a napkin, the way you bring things to people you love.

The dog stopped barking. Or maybe I stopped hearing it. The difference, at 3 AM, doesn't matter.

---

I think about the weight of small things. The weight of a peeling, curling on a newspaper. The weight of a photograph in a box labeled *MISC*. The weight of a dog's bark in the dark, announcing itself to no one, to everyone, to the indifferent universe.

My daughter is grown now. She lives three states away. She calls on Sundays, and we talk about nothing, and everything, the way you do when you're trying to hold something together across distance. Last time, she mentioned that she'd started peeling apples. *I think of you,* she said. *When I do it.*

I cried after we hung up. I don't know why. Or I know too many reasons. The apple I'd peeled that morning sat on my counter, browning at the edges, the spiral of skin dried and brittle beside it. I threw it away. I should have kept it. I should have pressed it in a book, or framed it, or simply left it there as evidence—*here, I was here, I did this, I made something small and continuous and true.*

But I threw it away. And then I peeled another one. And another. The knife in my hand, the fruit turning, the skin falling away in a curl. The small things. The weight of them. The way they accumulate, layer by layer, until you are who you are, until you are held together by nothing more than the continuous spiral of your own attention, your own care, your own refusal to let the knife slip, to let the cut go too deep, to let the darkness win.

The dog barks. I make tea. I peel an apple. I lay the skin on the cutting board like a question mark, like a promise.

Tomorrow, I will do it again.
